issues.issue: The execution date is left as "July ¥, 2005", so the "Effective Date" — the anchor for the Employment Term, the commission period and the severance end-date — is not legible on the face of the instrument. That is a mechanical defect that a court could be asked to fix by extrinsic evidence.

The preamble makes both Ajuba and Ajuba India jointly the "Company", yet Section 2.1 has only Ajuba India employ him and Sections 2.2/8.4 make only Ajuba India the payor. Which entity owes the obligations is arguable.

This states that "the Company" (both entities) employs the Employee, while Section 2.1 states that Ajuba India employs him as President of Ajuba India. The identity of the employer is left inconsistent.

"Board" is Ajuba's board, but Section 2.1 has the Employee report "directly to the Board (or selected designee of the Board of Directors of the Parent)" and Schedule 2.1 says he reports to the Chairman. The reporting line is not uniform.

The definition ends with the open catch-alls "such other entities serviced by the Company" and "other related services" after a long enumerated list, so the outer boundary of "Business" — the term that fixes the reach of the Article V noncompete — is uncertain. That is a classic ejusdem generis / general-vs-specific problem.
"Code" is defined but never used anywhere in the operative text, which is surplusage rather than a conflict.

"Known to the Employee as a consequence of or through the Employee's employment" makes ownership turn on how knowledge was acquired, a boundary that cannot be applied to ideas the Employee brought with him or learned independently. The phrase is vague on its face.

Section 4.1 assigns technology "conceived, developed or acquired during the Employment Term", a different trigger from this definition's "known to the Employee as a consequence of" his employment. The two capture different bodies of material.

"All information, in whatever form, regarding Parent, the Company their Business and their clients" is unbounded, and the ten enumerated categories are introduced by "without limitation", leaving the catch-all's reach against the specifics unsettled. There is also no carve-out in the definition itself for public or independently known information.

The definition is internally tangled: limb (a) already covers everything provided to healthcare-industry entities, which appears to swallow the quantitative test in limb (b), and limb (b)(ii)'s "more than the sum of (A) ... and (B)" formula is hard to apply. The scope of "Core Business" is genuinely uncertain.

The lookback periods run from "the date of termination of this Agreement", but it is the Employee's employment, not the Agreement, that terminates, and "actively sought" and "material contact" are undefined. The class of protected Customers is therefore imprecise.

Disputes over EBITDA are committed to "the independent accountants regularly employed by Ajuba", a one-sided mechanism whose finality (binding? appealable?) is not stated. A court could be asked whether that determination forecloses a bonus claim.

This runs the Term to "the third anniversary of this Agreement" while Section 8.1 runs it to "the third anniversary of the Effective Date"; with an illegible execution date those need not coincide. The mismatch also drives the Restricted Period in Section 1.14.

"Three years after the end of the Employment Term" is ambiguous where employment ends early: the end may be the actual termination date or the scheduled third anniversary under Section 1.9. That difference can move the expiry of the Article V covenants by years.

The section commands "full professional and business-related time, skills and best efforts" and duties "customarily performed by a President", then permits unspecified passive investments and outside board seats, leaving the line between permitted and forbidden activity indistinct. "Customarily performed by a President" has no fixed content.

Schedule 2.1 is stated to control over the Bylaws and yet is "deemed to have been amended" by any consolidation or outsourcing described in Section 8.4(a), so the duties that fix a Good Reason "material diminution" can be unilaterally rewritten. The interaction with Section 8.4(a) is not coherent.

The salary step-up is "retroactive to the first business day of the year following the Fiscal Year in which such EBITDA was achieved", which is retroactive to a future date and does not say whether the trigger applies once or in any year. The escalation date is genuinely unclear.

The Allowance is paid "in lieu of receiving health, dental and other benefits afforded to Ajuba US employees", while Section 2.2(c) entitles the Employee to participate in all benefit plans made available to senior executives. The two benefit entitlements are hard to reconcile.

The Employee is only "eligible to receive" the Bonus and the table gives discrete EBITDA points with no rule for results between or above the tiers or for prorating. Whether a Bonus is earned at all, and in what amount, is left open.

The final sentence conditions the FY2007 Bonus on service "through the entire Employment Term" unless terminated under Sections 8.3 or 8.4, while Sections 8.2 and 8.5 disclaim liability for any bonus "for either the prior or current year". The carve-outs and disclaimers do not line up.

Benefits may be "modified or discontinued at the sole discretion of the Company", yet Section 8.4(c) makes a breach of the Section 2.2 benefit provisions Good Reason for the Employee to resign with full severance. The unfettered discretion and the Good Reason trigger pull against each other.

"Substantially similar to the D&O Policy maintained by the Company immediately prior to the date hereof" gives no measure of similarity (limits, retention, tail coverage). The benchmark policy is not attached or described.

The clause turns on undefined terms — "Samii", "net sales", contracts "generated by" a party, and the date an Eligible Contract "goes live" — none of which is defined anywhere in the Agreement. Each is a live candidate for construction.

Commissions are payable only if the Employee "is employed by the Company as of the Payment Date", yet Sections 8.3 and 8.4 cross-refer to "Section 2.2(e)" as the source of post-termination Reorganization Bonus rights. The cross-reference does not fit this subsection.

Payment is conditioned on the Employee being employed "or had been terminated by the Company pursuant to Section 8.3 or 8.4", which omits a Section 8.4 resignation for Good Reason — a termination by the Employee, not the Company. Whether the bonus survives that route is arguable.

The Reorganization Bonus is created here in Section 2.2(f), but Sections 8.3 and 8.4 both preserve it "in accordance with Section 2.2(e)", which is the Commissions subsection. The cross-reference is wrong on its face.
"Legitimate business purposes" is an undefined and elastic exception that could swallow the Company's confidentiality promise entirely. Nothing in the Agreement supplies a benchmark for legitimacy.

Assignment operates only "upon the Company's request", so title does not pass automatically, and the material captured extends to anything "relating in any way to the Business" — a far wider class than the Section 1.4 definition of Company Technology. The reach of the assignment is uncertain.

The covenant bars "any activity which is in competition with the Business" anywhere in the United States and India for three years past the Term, with a residual "or otherwise" after the list of capacities; both the activity and the capacity limits are open-ended. This is the provision on which any enforcement fight would turn.

Section 9.8 preserves "that certain Non-Competition Agreement of even date herewith to which Employee is also subject", so a second, separate noncompete governs the same conduct and its relation to this one is unstated. Which instrument controls is a genuine question.

The restriction runs for the whole Restricted Period but "Customer" in Section 1.7 is fixed by reference to the six- and twelve-month windows before termination, so the two time frames are not aligned. The overlap is workable but not obvious.

The sentence stacks two different prohibitions with an "or, with respect to any employee in the United States or any employee in India having the title of Supervisor and above" qualifier whose reach across the preceding clauses is unclear. The following sentence's reference to "the preceding sentence" compounds the problem.

The substitution of "Core Business" applies "for purposes of subsection (a) above only" after a Section 8.4 termination, leaving subsections (b) and (c) tied to the broader "Business". Whether that narrowing was intended to be so partial is arguable.

Section 8.4 covers both Company termination and Employee resignation for Good Reason or any other reason, so it is unclear whether an ordinary resignation also triggers this narrowing while Section 8.5 resignations do not. The two termination routes overlap.

The Employee warrants he is subject to no noncompete "except for this Agreement", yet Section 9.8 records a separate Non-Competition Agreement of even date to which he is also subject. The representation and Section 9.8 point in different directions.

The article invokes "Articles I, IV or V" (Article I is Definitions, plainly meant to be Article III) and refers to "the Company's rights under Article VII hereof", which is this very article rather than Article VIII. Both are cross-reference errors that change which breaches carry equitable relief.
Section 8.1 fixes the outside date as "the third anniversary of the Effective Date" while Section 1.9 uses "the third anniversary of this Agreement". The two anchors are stated differently.

Subsection (a) piles specifics onto the vague standard "conduct causing the Company or its subsidiaries substantial public disgrace or disrepute", and the cure paragraph gives fifteen days to cure "such failure" without saying which of the four grounds are curable. Both the disgrace limb and the cure right are open to construction.

Subsection (c) makes breach of "Articles I, IV, V or VI" Cause, but Article I is the definitions article and cannot be breached; Article III (confidentiality) is evidently intended. The list does not match the instrument.

"Disability" requires substantial failure to perform essential duties for 120 days in any 240-day period "as determined by competent medical evidence" without saying who selects the physician or how the count is made. The trigger is workable but not self-executing.

The section preserves the Reorganization Bonus "in accordance with Section 2.2(e)", but the Reorganization Bonus is created by Section 2.2(f); Section 2.2(e) is the Commissions clause. The cross-reference is erroneous.

The severance measure — "the compensation at the rate or level, as applicable, in effect on the date of such termination, through the third anniversary of the Effective Date" — does not say whether "compensation" means Base Salary only or also the Allowance, Bonus and commissions. That is the central money question in the clause.

The second sentence lets the Employee terminate "for Good Reason or for any other reason pursuant to this Section 8.4", which on its face gives full severance for any resignation, while Section 8.5 lets him resign for any reason and receive only accrued Base Salary. The two sections cannot both be right.

This section gives an Employee who resigns for any reason only accrued Base Salary, yet Section 8.4 states he may terminate "for Good Reason or for any other reason pursuant to this Section 8.4" and receive severance through the third anniversary. The routes for a voluntary resignation conflict.

Section 9.2 simply drops an unenforceable provision, while Article VII directs a court to modify overbroad restrictions and enforce them as modified. The two savings mechanisms differ for the Article V covenants.

The first sentence addresses waiver generally, but the second limits the effect of "such written waiver", although no writing requirement was imposed anywhere in the clause. The drafting leaves it unclear whether an oral or implied waiver can ever operate.

"The Company" is defined as two entities, so it is unclear whether a merger or asset sale by only one of them permits assignment, and the closing sentence binds "successors and assigns" despite the preceding restriction. Whether a successor can enforce the covenants is a real question.
The notice block gives an address only for Ajuba International, Inc., though Ajuba India is an equal party and the payor under Sections 2.2 and 8.4. Service on the India entity is unprovided for.

Withholding is limited to "federal, state and local taxes", but the payor under Sections 2.2 and 8.4 is Ajuba India paying an India-resident employee, whose taxes are not US federal, state or local. The clause does not fit the payment structure.

The clause preserves "the ongoing provisions of this Agreement" without identifying them or supplying any test for which provisions are ongoing. Which of Articles III, IV and V survive, and for how long, is left to inference.

The integration clause carves out "that certain Non-Competition Agreement of even date herewith", leaving a second restrictive-covenant instrument operating alongside Article V with no stated priority. The relationship between the two noncompetes is unresolved.

The clause turns on "the Parties", a capitalised term defined only in the separate Separation Agreement and never in this Agreement, and confers beneficiary status on Parent without saying which rights Parent may enforce. The extent of Parent's standing is unclear.

Michigan law is chosen, but the employer and payor is an Indian company employing an India-resident under Section 2.1, and Section 8.2(d) requires him to reside in India. Whether Michigan law can govern the India employment relationship is arguable.
"Disparage" is undefined and the obligation runs "thereafter" without end, so its boundary against truthful or legally required statements cannot be fixed. The sentence also ends without punctuation.

This imposes a perpetual mutual non-disparagement duty, while paragraph 3 of the attached Separation Agreement limits the Employee's duty to the period "[f]or so long as Employee holds Restricted Stock Units" and carves out statements to the Board. The two cannot both measure the same duty.

"May be brought against any of parties in the courts of the State of Michigan" is permissive in form yet coupled with consent to jurisdiction and a venue waiver, so whether the clause is exclusive or merely consensual is genuinely contestable. That is the classic mandatory-versus-permissive forum question.
The party block is a blank form — the Employee's name is missing — so the instrument as attached identifies no releasor. It is a form defect rather than a substantive ambiguity.
The recital breaks off with a blank where the Employment Agreement date should appear, leaving the released agreement unidentified on the face of the form. The sentence is incomplete.
The recital ends with a blank effective date of termination, which is the date the release period in paragraph 1 is measured to. As drafted it states nothing.

This recital says only that the Employee was given the "opportunity" to consult counsel, while operative paragraph 8 states that he was advised to and "did so". The recital and the operative acknowledgment do not match.

The release sweeps "any and all" claims "known or unknown" through a long enumerated statute list introduced by "including, but not limited to", then carves out only claims "to compel the payment of amounts due to Employee as provided in the Employment Agreement". Both the reach of the catch-all and the width of that single carve-out are open to construction.

The carve-out preserves claims for amounts due under the Employment Agreement, yet paragraph 19 releases the Company from "all of its remaining obligations" if the Employee breaches, and Section 8.4 conditions severance on this very release. The interlocking conditions are not fully reconciled.

The defined bundle "Company Information and Property" ends with the catch-all "all other assets, materials and information of any kind or nature, belonging or pertaining to Company", whose reach against the enumerated items is uncertain. "Pertaining to" has no boundary.

The Employee's obligation runs only "[f]or so long as Employee holds Restricted Stock Units", a term used nowhere else in this instrument or the Employment Agreement, yet the same sentence says he "shall never" disparage. The duration is both undefined and self-contradictory.

The Company's counter-promise addresses "the circumstances of Employee's resignation", although the release is drafted for any termination, and Section 9.13 of the Employment Agreement imposes an unconditional mutual duty. The two non-disparagement regimes differ in scope and duration.

The paragraph is a sentence fragment — "To never seek or accept employment with Company" has no subject or operative verb — so it is unclear who promises what. The grammatical defect goes to whether any obligation was created.

This preserves the Employment Agreement's confidentiality, proprietary-rights and noncompete obligations, but paragraph 15 says the release "contains the entire agreement between Employee and Company regarding the matters set forth herein". The interaction of the two is workable but not seamless.

"A reasonable amount of the Employee's time" and "reasonable notice" set no limit on the cooperation demanded, and reimbursement is for "lost wages" without a rate. The obligation's outer bound cannot be applied.

The revocation notice must be sent or delivered to addresses that are left blank in the form, so the prescribed method of revocation cannot be performed as written. Whether a revocation otherwise communicated is effective would have to be construed.

This paragraph says the Release "is not effective until this revocation period has expired", while paragraph 11 makes the Company's obligations contingent on the Employee also giving written confirmation that he did not revoke. The two conditions to effectiveness differ.

"The Company's obligations" is not identified — it may mean only severance or every obligation in the Release — and the required "written confirmation" has no deadline or form. The condition precedent is imprecise.

The Company may disclose the terms "only for legitimate business purposes", an undefined standard that gives the Company a broad and unmeasurable exception to a confidentiality promise binding the Employee absolutely. The asymmetry invites construction against the drafter.
"Regarding the matters set forth herein" limits the integration to unstated subject matter, leaving unclear what prior understandings survive. The qualifier does the work but is not defined.

This paragraph directs judicial reformation of any invalid provision, while Section 9.2 of the Employment Agreement leaves an invalid provision simply severed. The two savings clauses in the same package operate differently.

The forfeiture is of the Company's obligations "under the Severance Agreement", a term used nowhere else — this instrument is defined as the "Release" and the pay obligation sits in Section 8.4 of the Employment Agreement. The sentence also ends in a comma, unfinished.

Releasing the Company of "all of its remaining obligations" on any violation cuts against paragraph 1's carve-out preserving the Employee's claims for amounts due under the Employment Agreement. Which prevails on a minor breach is unresolved.

The heading describes him as "President of International Operations" whereas Section 2.1 gives the titles President of Ajuba India and President-International for Ajuba. The titles are stated inconsistently.

This gives him responsibility for Finance/Accounting/Cash Management across Ajuba US and all subsidiaries, yet Section 8.4(a) provides that consolidating, eliminating or outsourcing exactly those functions is not a material diminution, and Section 2.1 deems the Schedule amended accordingly. The duty and the carve-out pull against each other.

The Schedule has him report to the Chairman of the Board, while Section 2.1 requires him to "report directly to the Board (or selected designee of the Board of Directors of the Parent)" — and Section 2.1 makes the Schedule control over conflicts only with the Bylaws. The reporting line conflicts.

Section 2.2(f) conditions the $200,000 on the Novi office being "restructured", while the Schedule reduces the Employee's task to overseeing termination of the Novi lease. What counts as the restructuring is stated at two different levels.

Section 2.2(f) recites that Schedule I "sets forth the specific cost savings for each action and a reasonable risk assessment", while this paragraph disclaims any representation or warranty as to cost savings or client reaction. The operative bonus condition and the disclaimer point in different directions.

Costs are made "the sole responsibility of Ajuba", yet Section 2.2(f) makes Ajuba India the payor of the Reorganization Bonus and the Agreement defines "Company" as both entities. Which entity bears the closure costs is stated inconsistently with the rest of the package.
